title: Ludwigia hyssopifolia: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Ludwigia hyssopifolia in Rice: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Ludwigia hyssopifolia can cut rice yield by up to 81 percent. Learn to spot this kahoy kahoy weed and meet the beetle that helps you fight it.
excerpt: Ludwigia hyssopifolia is an upright, yellow flowered broadleaf weed that farmers call Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina. It grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it, how much harm it can do, and how to control it before it spreads.

blocks.text:
In English, Ludwigia hyssopifolia is called seedbox. It belongs to the evening primrose family, Onagraceae. In the bukid, farmers know it as Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina. These names also cover other Ludwigia weeds, so you need to check the plant closely. Being a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You will find it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. Some plants live as annuals and die after one season, while others keep going as perennials. It spreads by seed and also by propagules, which are plant parts that can grow into new plants. Its slender, reddish pods hold the seeds that refill the soil for the next cropping.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Ludwigia hyssopifolia
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Look for an upright, branched plant up to 60 cm tall. The stems are angled, green to reddish, and turn woody near the base. Its leaves are narrow and lance shaped. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The yellow flowers have four diamond shaped petals and eight stamens, more than the number of sepals. After flowering, it forms slender, four angled, reddish seed pods.

items: Upright, branched plants up to 60 cm tall standing among the young palay.
Angled stems, green to reddish, that feel woody and hard near the base.
Narrow, lance shaped leaves growing along the stems and branches.
Yellow flowers with four diamond shaped petals and eight stamens inside.
Slender, reddish seed pods with four angles forming after the flowers.
Look alike tip: Ludwigia octovalvis has much bigger yellow flowers, while Ludwigia perennis has as many stamens as sepals.

blocks.text:
Ludwigia hyssopifolia is a C3 weed of rice, the same as the rice plant itself. It invades many kinds of rice culture, and it grows on both clay loam and clay soils. That means it can show up on many kinds of rice farms.

When it is left to compete fully, the losses are heavy. At a ratio of 4 to 1, weed to rice, rice yield can drop by 64 percent. At a ratio of 8 to 1, the loss can reach 81 percent. Those numbers show why early weeding pays off. Each plant left standing also drops seeds that keep the problem alive for the next season.

blocks.title: Its weak spot
blocks.text: Nature gives you a helper here. A small leaf beetle called Altica, from the chrysomelid family, attacks this weed. Both the larvae and the adult beetles eat its leaves hungrily. So if you see small beetles chewing holes in kahoy kahoy leaves, leave them alone. Avoid spraying insecticide where they feed, because that kills your helper too.

items: Pull young plants before the woody base forms, because older plants with hard, woody stems are tough to uproot by hand.
Remove plants before the reddish seed pods ripen, and carry them out of the paddy so the seeds do not drop on the mud.
Leave the Altica leaf beetles alone when you see them chewing kahoy kahoy leaves, since they weaken the weed for free.
Since it can live on as a perennial, check bunds and field edges after harvest and remove any old plants still growing there.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Ludwigia hyssopifolia down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Ludwigia hyssopifolia Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Ludwigia hyssopifolia

items.q: What is Ludwigia hyssopifolia called in Tagalog?
items.a: Farmers call it Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina. Its English name is seedbox. These local names are shared with other Ludwigia weeds, such as the taller Mexican primrose willow and the shorter perennial water primrose. So look at the flowers. This one has yellow flowers with four diamond shaped petals and eight stamens.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first. Use clean seed, level the field well, and keep shallow water where you can. Hand weed early, before the pods ripen. If you need a herbicide, pick one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label. Also protect the Altica beetles that feed on it.

items.q: How much yield can this weed take from my rice?
items.a: A lot, if you leave it alone. Under full competition, a ratio of 4 weeds to 1 rice plant can cut yield by 64 percent. At 8 weeds to 1 rice plant, the loss can reach 81 percent. That is why early weeding is worth the effort, even in fields that look only a little weedy.
